analysis.one_liner: Lets the FTC sue to win refunds for people cheated by deceptive companies.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a committee vote: it was referred to the Senate Commerce Committee on December 15, 2021, sat there without action, and died when the Congress ended on January 3, 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: In 2021 the Supreme Court ruled that the FTC could no longer win refunds or restitution for consumers in its federal court cases, leaving the agency able to stop a scam but not return victims' money. This bill restores that power: courts could order refunds, contract rescission, and disgorgement of ill-gotten gains in FTC deception cases, subject to a three-year deadline and a requirement that the FTC prove a reasonable consumer relied on the deception and was harmed. It also lets the Justice Department sue for damages on behalf of Americans injured by antitrust violations.
analysis.who_benefits: Consumers cheated by deceptive companies — fake 'free trial' subscription traps, fraudulent health or money-making claims, and similar schemes — would be able to get their money back through FTC lawsuits, which currently cannot return money to victims [S2][S3]. Americans overcharged because of antitrust violations would gain a new avenue of recovery through Justice Department lawsuits brought on their behalf [S2][S3].

how_it_helps.text: Restores the FTC's power to ask courts to order restitution for consumer loss, rescission or reformation of contracts, refunds of property, and disgorgement of profits from unfair or deceptive practices [S2][S3].
Gives victims a three-year window to obtain this relief, a window that does not count time when the company being sued is outside the United States [S3].

Adds a new Section 4A(b) to the Clayton Act letting the Attorney General sue in federal court on behalf of U.S. residents injured by antitrust violations, recovering their damages and the cost of the suit, without any minimum dollar amount [S3].
Lets the FTC refer a won competition case to the Attorney General to collect actual damages under the Clayton Act [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Companies that engage in deceptive practices would bear the cost: they could be ordered to return consumers' money and give up profits gained from violations [S3]. Companies that violate antitrust laws would face new damages suits brought by the Justice Department on behalf of consumers [S3].
analysis.who_pays_short: Companies that deceive or overcharge consumers

drawbacks.text: The FTC would have to prove that a reasonable individual knew the practice was unfair or deceptive, materially relied on it, and was proximately harmed by it — and the court may not presume reliance just because a consumer was exposed to the practice. Proving consumer-by-consumer reliance could make many restitution cases much harder to win [S3].

Redress and disgorgement claims would face a three-year deadline from the violation, and disgorgement would be capped at net profits directly related to the violation and offset by any restitution ordered, shrinking what companies would have to pay back [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For people scammed out of money, the bill restores a remedy that does not exist today, which is a real gain even with the narrower three-year window and the reliance-proof hurdles. The 'due process' conditions are the price of the bill's design: they favor companies accused of deception by making it harder and slower for the FTC to win restitution, so the restored power would cover fewer cases than the FTC's authority before the 2021 Supreme Court ruling. On balance it helps consumers more than it hurts them, but it is a deliberately restrained version of consumer redress.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in December 2021 and sent to the Senate Commerce Committee, which never took it up, and it expired when the two-year Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Mike Lee introduced the bill on December 15, 2021, joined as original cosponsors by Sens. Lummis, Tillis, and Hawley, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation [S1][S3][S5].
Five Republicans in total cosponsored the bill; no Democrat did [S4].
The action history shows no further steps: no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, and no floor action for the remainder of the 117th Congress [S5].

The bill responds to a real gap: after the Supreme Court's 2021 AMG Capital Management v. FTC decision, the FTC could no longer obtain monetary redress for consumers under the statute it uses in deception cases, a change widely discussed in consumer-protection policy debates.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Companies accused of deceiving consumers are better off, because the post-2021 status quo — in which FTC lawsuits can stop a practice but cannot return victims' money — remains in place. The bill's sponsor and cosponsors also avoided the constraints a committee process might have imposed, but they gained nothing tangible from a bill that never moved.

for.name: Mike Lee
for.role: U.S. Senator from Utah; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on December 15, 2021, proposing restored FTC redress powers with new proof requirements, and DOJ antitrust suits on behalf of consumers [S1][S3].

for.name: 5 of 50 Senate Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, including original cosponsors Lummis, Tillis, and Hawley [S3][S4].

against.name: Maria Cantwell
against.role: Chair, Senate Commerce, Science, and Transportation Committee
against.what_they_did: As chair of the committee the bill was referred to, took no action on it — no hearing, markup, or vote — for the rest of the Congress [S5].

sides.party_line_note: There were no votes to measure; all six sponsors and cosponsors were Republicans and the bill died in a committee chaired by a Democrat, but no one ever voted on or publicly opposed it.

industries.industry: Companies facing FTC deception cases (scam operators, subscription and 'free trial' marketers)
industries.note: Under the bill they could be ordered to refund victims and disgorge profits, restoring exposure they lost after the Supreme Court's 2021 AMG Capital ruling. The bill's reliance-proof and three-year limits would temper that exposure [S3].
The Justice Department could sue for damages on behalf of U.S. residents injured by antitrust violations, adding a federal plaintiff on top of private and state suits [S3].
